title: India's Supreme Court Just Upheld a 28% Tax on Every Rupee Bet on Online Games. The Bill Could Exceed ₹1 Lakh Crore.
excerpt: The ruling validates retrospective GST demands on Dream11, MPL, and over 100 gaming companies, ending a legal battle that goes back to the industry's earliest days.
body:
The Supreme Court of India has ruled that online gaming companies must pay 28 per cent GST on the full face value of every bet placed on their platforms — not just the commission or platform fee they retain. The judgment, delivered last week, validates the government's position in one of the largest tax disputes in India's technology sector and opens the door to retrospective tax demands that could exceed ₹1 lakh crore.

The ruling is a decisive blow to an industry that had built its legal defence on the distinction between games of skill and games of chance.

## The Core Dispute

The fight centred on a deceptively simple question: when a user deposits ₹100 on a fantasy sports platform like Dream11, should the government tax the entire ₹100, or only the ₹10 the platform keeps as commission?

Before the GST law was amended in 2023, most gaming companies paid 18 per cent GST on their platform fee — the Gross Gaming Revenue (GGR) model. Under that approach, the tax on a ₹100 deposit was roughly ₹1.80. The Directorate General of GST Intelligence took a different view, arguing the full deposit amount constituted the taxable value. That interpretation pushed the tax to ₹28 — a fifteen-fold increase.

The Supreme Court sided with the tax authorities. Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan held that online games involving monetary stakes on uncertain outcomes qualify as betting and gambling under the GST framework, regardless of the level of skill involved. The court also ruled that the 2023 amendments were "clarificatory" rather than substantive — meaning the 28 per cent rate applies retroactively to earlier periods.

## Who Gets Hit

The verdict restores a ₹21,000 crore tax notice against Gameskraft Technologies and exposes dozens of other companies to similar demands. Dream11, Mobile Premier League, WinZO, Games24x7, and more than 100 other operators now face potential tax liabilities dating back years.

Delta Corp, India's only listed casino operator, saw its shares fall sharply after the ruling. Nazara Technologies, which has exposure to the gaming ecosystem, also came under pressure.

Industry analysts estimate that the total retrospective tax exposure across the sector could exceed ₹1 lakh crore — a sum that would be existential for many mid-tier platforms and trigger a wave of consolidation. Reports already suggest that Dream11 is looking to acquire distressed competitors at steep discounts.

## The Vodafone Echo

The retrospective dimension has inevitably drawn comparisons with India's most notorious tax dispute. In the Vodafone case, the government amended the Income Tax Act retroactively to pursue a tax demand that the Supreme Court had already ruled against. That episode damaged India's reputation with foreign investors for years.

Gaming companies had argued that the 2023 GST amendments fundamentally changed the tax treatment and should not apply to earlier periods. The Supreme Court disagreed, finding that the amendments merely clarified what the law had always intended.

## What It Means for NRIs

India's real-money gaming market had attracted significant foreign investment, with several NRI-founded or NRI-backed companies among the major players. The ruling introduces deep uncertainty about the viability of existing business models and the safety of capital already deployed.

For the millions of Indian diaspora users who play fantasy cricket on Dream11 during the IPL or wager on card games through MPL, the ruling is unlikely to change the user experience immediately. But it will reshape the economics of the platforms they use — potentially leading to higher entry fees, reduced prize pools, or the exit of smaller players from the market.

The ruling also sends a broader signal about India's regulatory posture toward technology-driven industries. In an ecosystem still processing the aftershocks of the startup funding winter, the prospect of ₹1 lakh crore in retrospective tax demands will give pause to investors evaluating India's gaming, fintech, and platform economy sectors.

Sources: Supreme Court of India, LiveLaw, Inc42, The Indian Eye, Trade Brains
